claim: Nerve tissue contains a high density of chemical synapses, about 1 per µm3 in the mammalian cerebral cortex.
source: Nerve tissue contains a high density of chemical synapses, about 1 per µm3 in the mammalian cerebral cortex.
evidence: This is a factual statement about synapse density in mammalian cortex, supported by established scientific knowledge and consistent with cited literature.

claim: SynEM yields 97% precision and recall in binary cortical connectomes with no user interaction.
source: SynEM yields 97% precision and recall in binary cortical connectomes with no user interaction.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: One cubic millimeter of gray matter in the mouse cerebral cortex contains at least 4 kilometers of axons.
source: One cubic millimeter of gray matter in the mouse cerebral cortex, spanning the entire depth of the gray matter and comprising several presumed cortical columns (Figure 1a), for example, contains at least 4 kilometers of axons, about 1 kilometer of dendritic shafts, about 1 billion spines (contributing an additional 2–3 kilometers of spine neck path length) and about 1 billion synapses (Figure 1b).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Figure 1b and references to established literature on cortical anatomy.

claim: One cubic millimeter of gray matter in the mouse cerebral cortex contains about 1 kilometer of dendritic shafts.
source: One cubic millimeter of gray matter in the mouse cerebral cortex, spanning the entire depth of the gray matter and comprising several presumed cortical columns (Figure 1a), for example, contains at least 4 kilometers of axons, about 1 kilometer of dendritic shafts, about 1 billion spines (contributing an additional 2–3 kilometers of spine neck path length) and about 1 billion synapses (Figure 1b).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Figure 1b and references to established literature on cortical anatomy.

claim: One cubic millimeter of gray matter in the mouse cerebral cortex contains about 1 billion spines.
source: One cubic millimeter of gray matter in the mouse cerebral cortex, spanning the entire depth of the gray matter and comprising several presumed cortical columns (Figure 1a), for example, contains at least 4 kilometers of axons, about 1 kilometer of dendritic shafts, about 1 billion spines (contributing an additional 2–3 kilometers of spine neck path length) and about 1 billion synapses (Figure 1b).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Figure 1b and references to established literature on cortical anatomy.

claim: One cubic millimeter of gray matter in the mouse cerebral cortex contains about 1 billion synapses.
source: One cubic millimeter of gray matter in the mouse cerebral cortex, spanning the entire depth of the gray matter and comprising several presumed cortical columns (Figure 1a), for example, contains at least 4 kilometers of axons, about 1 kilometer of dendritic shafts, about 1 billion spines (contributing an additional 2–3 kilometers of spine neck path length) and about 1 billion synapses (Figure 1b).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Figure 1b and references to established literature on cortical anatomy.

claim: Manual neurite contouring proceeds at 200–400 work hours per millimeter neurite path length.
source: when comparing the contouring of neurites (proceeding at 200–400 work hours per millimeter neurite path length) with synapse annotation by manually searching the volumetric data for synaptic junctions (Figure 1d, proceeding at about 0.1 hr per µm3), synapse annotation consumed at least 20-fold less annotation time than neurite reconstruction (Figure 1c).
evidence: This is an estimate of annotation time based on established practices in the field.

claim: Manual synapse annotation by volume search proceeds at about 0.1 hr per µm3.
source: when comparing the contouring of neurites (proceeding at 200–400 work hours per millimeter neurite path length) with synapse annotation by manually searching the volumetric data for synaptic junctions (Figure 1d, proceeding at about 0.1 hr per µm3), synapse annotation consumed at least 20-fold less annotation time than neurite reconstruction (Figure 1c).
evidence: This is an estimate of annotation time based on the test set annotation in this study.

claim: Synapse annotation consumed at least 20-fold less annotation time than neurite reconstruction using manual contouring.
source: when comparing the contouring of neurites (proceeding at 200–400 work hours per millimeter neurite path length) with synapse annotation by manually searching the volumetric data for synaptic junctions (Figure 1d, proceeding at about 0.1 hr per µm3), synapse annotation consumed at least 20-fold less annotation time than neurite reconstruction (Figure 1c).
evidence: This is a calculation based on the annotation time estimates provided in the text.

claim: Axon-focused synapse annotation reduces synapse annotation time by about 8-fold for dense reconstructions.
source: This axon-focused synapse annotation reduces synapse annotation time by about 8-fold for dense reconstructions (proceeding at about 1 min per potential contact indicated by a vesicle accumulation, which occurs every about 4–10 µm along axons in mouse cortex).
evidence: This is an estimate based on the frequency of vesicle accumulations along axons and annotation time per contact.

claim: Vesicle accumulation occurs every about 4–10 µm along axons in mouse cortex.
source: This axon-focused synapse annotation reduces synapse annotation time by about 8-fold for dense reconstructions (proceeding at about 1 min per potential contact indicated by a vesicle accumulation, which occurs every about 4–10 µm along axons in mouse cortex).
evidence: This is a factual statement about axonal anatomy in mouse cortex, based on established knowledge.

claim: Skeleton reconstruction together with automated volume segmentations allows to proceed at about 7–10 hr per mm path length in mouse retina.
source: Skeleton reconstruction (Helmstaedter et al., 2011) together with automated volume segmentations (Helmstaedter et al., 2013; Berning et al., 2015), allow to proceed at about 7–10 hr per mm path length (mouse retina, Helmstaedter et al., 2013) or 4–7 hr per mm (mouse cortex, Berning et al., 2015), thus about 50-fold faster than manual contouring.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous work (Helmstaedter et al., 2011, 2013; Berning et al., 2015).

claim: Skeleton reconstruction together with automated volume segmentations allows to proceed at about 4–7 hr per mm path length in mouse cortex.
source: Skeleton reconstruction (Helmstaedter et al., 2011) together with automated volume segmentations (Helmstaedter et al., 2013; Berning et al., 2015), allow to proceed at about 7–10 hr per mm path length (mouse retina, Helmstaedter et al., 2013) or 4–7 hr per mm (mouse cortex, Berning et al., 2015), thus about 50-fold faster than manual contouring.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous work (Helmstaedter et al., 2011, 2013; Berning et al., 2015).

claim: Skeleton reconstruction with automated volume segmentations is about 50-fold faster than manual contouring.
source: Skeleton reconstruction (Helmstaedter et al., 2011) together with automated volume segmentations (Helmstaedter et al., 2013; Berning et al., 2015), allow to proceed at about 7–10 hr per mm path length (mouse retina, Helmstaedter et al., 2013) or 4–7 hr per mm (mouse cortex, Berning et al., 2015), thus about 50-fold faster than manual contouring.
evidence: This is a calculation based on the annotation times provided in the text.

claim: Recent improvements in online data delivery and visualization further reduce neurite reconstruction time by about 5–10 fold.
source: Recent improvements in online data delivery and visualization (Boergens et al., 2017) further reduce this by about 5–10 fold.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Boergens et al., 2017.

claim: Synapse detection has become a limiting step in dense large-scale connectomics.
source: Thus, synapse detection has become a limiting step in dense large-scale connectomics.
evidence: This is an inference based on the comparison of annotation times for neurite reconstruction and synapse detection.

claim: High-resolution EM micrographs are the gold standard for synapse detection.
source: High-resolution EM micrographs are the gold standard for synapse detection (Gray, 1959; Colonnier, 1968).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to foundational work in the field (Gray, 1959; Colonnier, 1968).

claim: Images acquired at about 2–4 nm in-plane resolution have been used to confirm chemical synapses using the characteristic intense heavy metal staining at the postsynaptic membrane.
source: Images acquired at about 2–4 nm in-plane resolution have been used to confirm chemical synapses using the characteristic intense heavy metal staining at the postsynaptic membrane, thought to be caused by the accumulated postsynaptic proteins ('postsynaptic density', PSD), and an agglomeration of synaptic vesicles at the membrane of the presynaptic terminal.
evidence: This is a description of established methods for synapse identification in EM, based on scientific knowledge.

claim: The intense heavy metal staining at the postsynaptic membrane is thought to be caused by the accumulated postsynaptic proteins ('postsynaptic density', PSD).
source: Images acquired at about 2–4 nm in-plane resolution have been used to confirm chemical synapses using the characteristic intense heavy metal staining at the postsynaptic membrane, thought to be caused by the accumulated postsynaptic proteins ('postsynaptic density', PSD), and an agglomeration of synaptic vesicles at the membrane of the presynaptic terminal.
evidence: This is a statement about the biological basis of EM contrast, based on established scientific knowledge.

claim: Synapses can be unequivocally identified in 2-dimensional images when cut perpendicularly to the synaptic cleft.
source: While synapses can be unequivocally identified in 2-dimensional images when cut perpendicularly to the synaptic cleft (Figure 1f), synapses at oblique orientations or with a synaptic cleft in-plane to the EM imaging are hard or impossible to identify.
evidence: This claim is supported by reference to Figure 1f and established knowledge about synapse identification in EM.

claim: Synapses at oblique orientations or with a synaptic cleft in-plane to the EM imaging are hard or impossible to identify.
source: While synapses can be unequivocally identified in 2-dimensional images when cut perpendicularly to the synaptic cleft (Figure 1f), synapses at oblique orientations or with a synaptic cleft in-plane to the EM imaging are hard or impossible to identify.
evidence: This is a statement about the challenges of synapse identification in EM, based on established knowledge.

claim: The usage of 3D EM imaging with a high resolution of 4–8 nm also in the cutting dimension (FIB/SEM) is ideal for synapse detection.
source: Therefore, the usage of 3D EM imaging with a high resolution of 4–8 nm also in the cutting dimension (FIB/SEM, Knott et al., 2008) is ideal for synapse detection.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Knott et al., 2008 and logical inference about the benefits of isotropic resolution.

claim: Automated synapse detection is available and successful for FIB-SEM data.
source: For such data, automated synapse detection is available and successful (Kreshuk et al., 2011; Becker et al., 2012, 2013, Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous work (Kreshuk et al., 2011; Becker et al., 2012, 2013).

claim: FIB-SEM currently does not scale to large volumes required for connectomics of the mammalian cerebral cortex.
source: However, FIB-SEM currently does not scale to large volumes required for connectomics of the mammalian cerebral cortex.
evidence: This is a statement about the limitations of FIB-SEM technology, based on established knowledge in the field.

claim: Serial Blockface EM (SBEM) scales to mm3-sized volumes.
source: Serial Blockface EM (SBEM, Denk and Horstmann, 2004) scales to such mm3 -sized volumes.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Denk and Horstmann, 2004 and established knowledge about SBEM capabilities.

claim: SBEM provides a resolution just sufficient to follow all axons in dense neuropil and to identify synapses across multiple sequential images.
source: However, SBEM provides a resolution just sufficient to follow all axons in dense neuropil and to identify synapses across multiple sequential images, independent of synapse orientation (Figure 1g, see also Synapse Gallery in Supplementary file 4; the resolution of SBEM is typically about 10 x 10 × 30 nm3; Figure 1g).
evidence: This claim is supported by reference to Figure 1g and Supplementary file 4, as well as established knowledge about SBEM resolution.

claim: The resolution of SBEM is typically about 10 x 10 × 30 nm3.
source: However, SBEM provides a resolution just sufficient to follow all axons in dense neuropil and to identify synapses across multiple sequential images, independent of synapse orientation (Figure 1g, see also Synapse Gallery in Supplementary file 4; the resolution of SBEM is typically about 10 x 10 × 30 nm3; Figure 1g).
evidence: This is a factual statement about SBEM resolution, based on established knowledge.

claim: Synapse detection methods developed for high-in plane resolution data do not provide the accuracy required for fully automated synapse detection in SBEM data.
source: In this setting, synapse detection methods developed for high-in plane resolution data do not provide the accuracy required for fully automated synapse detection (see below).
evidence: This claim is supported by data presented later in the manuscript comparing different methods.

claim: SynEM is an automated synapse detection method based on an automated segmentation of large-scale 3D EM data.
source: Here we report SynEM, an automated synapse detection method based on an automated segmentation of large-scale 3D EM data (using SegEM, Berning et al., 2015; an earlier version of SynEM was deposited on biorxiv, Staffler et al., 2017).
evidence: This is a description of the method reported in this study.

claim: SynEM achieves precision and recall for single-synapse detection of 88%.
source: SynEM achieves precision and recall for single-synapse detection of 88% and for binary neuron-to-neuron connectomes of 97% without any human interaction, essentially removing the synapse annotation challenge for large-scale mammalian connectomes.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by experimental data.

claim: SynEM achieves precision and recall for binary neuron-to-neuron connectomes of 97% without any human interaction.
source: SynEM achieves precision and recall for single-synapse detection of 88% and for binary neuron-to-neuron connectomes of 97% without any human interaction, essentially removing the synapse annotation challenge for large-scale mammalian connectomes.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by experimental data.

claim: SynEM considers synapse detection as a classification of interfaces between neuronal processes as synaptic or non-synaptic.
source: We consider synapse detection as a classification of interfaces between neuronal processes as synaptic or non-synaptic (Figure 2a; see also Mishchenko et al., 2010, Kreshuk et al., 2015, Huang et al., 2016).
evidence: This is a description of the approach used in SynEM, with reference to Figure 2a and citations to related work.

claim: The SynEM approach relies on a volume segmentation of the neuropil sufficient to provide locally continuous neurite pieces.
source: This approach relies on a volume segmentation of the neuropil sufficient to provide locally continuous neurite pieces (such as provided by SegEM, Berning et al., 2015, for SBEM data of mammalian cortex), for which the contact interfaces can be evaluated.
evidence: This is a description of the requirements for the SynEM approach, with citation to SegEM (Berning et al., 2015).

claim: Presynaptically, vesicle pools extend into the presynaptic terminal over at least 100–200 nm.
source: The unique features of synapses are distributed asymmetrically around the synaptic interface: presynaptically, vesicle pools extend into the presynaptic terminal over at least 100–200 nm; postsynaptically, the PSD has a width of about 20–30 nm.
evidence: This is a statement about the spatial extent of synaptic features, based on established knowledge of synapse ultrastructure.

claim: Postsynaptically, the PSD has a width of about 20–30 nm.
source: The unique features of synapses are distributed asymmetrically around the synaptic interface: presynaptically, vesicle pools extend into the presynaptic terminal over at least 100–200 nm; postsynaptically, the PSD has a width of about 20–30 nm.
evidence: This is a statement about the spatial extent of synaptic features, based on established knowledge of synapse ultrastructure.

claim: The SynEM classifier considers the subvolumes adjacent to the neurite interface explicitly and separately, up to distances of 40, 80, and 160 nm from the interface.
source: To account for this surround information our classifier considers the subvolumes adjacent to the neurite interface explicitly and separately, unlike previous approaches (Kreshuk et al., 2015; Huang et al., 2016), up to distances of 40, 80, and 160 nm from the interface, restricted to the two segments in question (Figure 2b; the interface itself was considered as an additional subvolume).
evidence: This is a description of the SynEM classifier design, with reference to Figure 2b and citations to previous approaches.

claim: SynEM computes a set of 11 texture features.
source: We then compute a set of 11 texture features (Table 1, this includes the raw data as one feature), and derive 9 simple aggregate statistics over the texture features within the 7 subvolumes.
evidence: This is a description of the features used in SynEM, with reference to Table 1.

claim: SynEM derives 9 simple aggregate statistics over the texture features within the 7 subvolumes.
source: We then compute a set of 11 texture features (Table 1, this includes the raw data as one feature), and derive 9 simple aggregate statistics over the texture features within the 7 subvolumes.
evidence: This is a description of the features used in SynEM, with reference to Table 1.

claim: SynEM employs 5 shape features calculated for the border subvolume and the two subvolumes extending 160 nm into the pre- and postsynaptic processes.
source: Furthermore, we employ 5 shape features calculated for the border subvolume and the two subvolumes extending 160 nm into the pre- and postsynaptic processes, respectively.
evidence: This is a description of the features used in SynEM.

claim: The feature vector for classification had 3224 entries for each interface.
source: Together, the feature vector for classification had 3224 entries for each interface (Table 1).
evidence: This is a description of the feature vector used in SynEM, with reference to Table 1.

claim: SynEM was developed and tested on a dataset from layer 4 of mouse primary somatosensory cortex acquired using SBEM.
source: We developed and tested SynEM on a dataset from layer 4 (L4) of mouse primary somatosensory cortex (S1) acquired using SBEM (dataset 2012-09-28_ex145_07x2, Boergens et al., unpublished; the dataset was also used in developing SegEM, Berning et al., 2015).
evidence: This is a description of the dataset used for SynEM development and testing.

claim: The dataset used for SynEM development had a size of 93 × 60 × 93 µm3 imaged at a voxel size of 11.24 × 11.24 × 28 nm3.
source: The dataset had a size of 93 × 60 × 93 µm3 imaged at a voxel size of 11.24 × 11.24 × 28 nm3.
evidence: This is a description of the dataset used for SynEM development and testing.

claim: The SynEM classifier was implemented to output a synapse score for each interface and each of the two possible pre-to-postsynaptic directions.
source: Then, the SynEM classifier was implemented to output a synapse score for each interface and each of the two possible pre-to-postsynaptic directions (Figure 3a–c).
evidence: This is a description of the SynEM classifier output, with reference to Figure 3a-c.

claim: The SynEM score was then thresholded to obtain an automated classification of interfaces into synaptic / non-synaptic.
source: The SynEM score was then thresholded to obtain an automated classification of interfaces into synaptic / non-synaptic (θ in Figure 3a).
evidence: This is a description of the SynEM classification procedure, with reference to Figure 3a.

claim: The SynEM scores for the two possible synaptic directions at a given neurite-to-neurite interface were rather disjunct in the range of relevant thresholds.
source: Since the SynEM scores for the two possible synaptic directions at a given neurite-to-neurite interface were rather disjunct in the range of relevant thresholds, we used the larger of the two scores for classification (Figure 3b; θs and θnn refer to the SynEM thresholds optimized for single synapse or neuron-to-neuron connectome reconstruction, respectively, see below).
evidence: This is a description of the SynEM score distribution, with reference to Figure 3b.

claim: A total of 75,383 interfaces (1858 synaptic, 73,525 non-synaptic) were annotated for SynEM training and validation.
source: A total of 75,383 interfaces (1858 synaptic, 73,525 non-synaptic) were annotated in image volumes drawn from 40 locations within the entire EM dataset (Figure 3—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is a description of the training and validation data for SynEM.

claim: About 80% of the labels (1467 synaptic, 61,619 non-synaptic) were used for training, the remaining were used for validation.
source: About 80% of the labels (1467 synaptic, 61,619 non-synaptic) were used for training, the remaining were used for validation.
evidence: This is a description of the training and validation data split for SynEM.

claim: The initial SynEM classifier provided only about 70% precision and recall.
source: Our initial classifier used the texture features from Kreshuk et al. (2011) with minor modifications and in addition the number of voxels of the interface and the two interfacing neurite segmentation objects (restricted to 160 nm distance from the interface) as a first shape feature (Table 1). This classifier provided only about 70% precision and recall (Figure 3d).
evidence: This is a description of the performance of the initial SynEM classifier, with reference to Figure 3d and Table 1.

claim: Extending the feature space and adding more subvolumes increased the SynEM classifier to about 75% precision and recall.
source: We then extended the feature space by adding more texture features capturing local image statistics (Table 1) and shape features. In particular, we added filters capturing local image variance in an attempt to represent the 'empty' appearance of postsynaptic spines, and the presynaptic vesicle clouds imposing as high-frequency high-variance features in the EM images. Also, we added more subvolumes over which features were aggregated (see Figure 2b), increasing the dimension of the feature space from 603 to 3224. Together with additional aggregate statistics, the classifier reached about 75% precision and recall.
evidence: This is a description of the improvements made to the SynEM classifier, with reference to Table 1 and Figure 2b.

claim: Switching from AdaBoostM1 to LogitBoost and using the directed label set yielded a precision and recall of 87% and 86% on the validation set.
source: A substantial improvement was obtained by switching from an ensemble of decision-stumps (one-level decision tree) trained by AdaBoostM1 (Freund and Schapire, 1997) as classifier to decision stumps trained by LogitBoost (Friedman et al., 2000). In addition, the directed label set proved to be superior. Together, these improvements yielded a precision and recall of 87% and 86% on the validation set (Figure 3d).
evidence: This is a description of the improvements made to the SynEM classifier, with reference to Figure 3d and citations to AdaBoostM1 and LogitBoost.

claim: The test set was a dense volume annotation of all synapses in a randomly positioned region containing dense neuropil of size 5.8 × 5.8 × 7.2 µm3 from the L4 mouse cortex dataset.
source: This test set was a dense volume annotation of all synapses in a randomly positioned region containing dense neuropil of size 5.8 × 5.8 × 7.2 µm3 from the L4 mouse cortex dataset.
evidence: This is a description of the test set used for SynEM evaluation.

claim: The test set contained 235 synapses and 20319 non-synaptic interfaces.
source: In total, the test set contained 235 synapses and 20319 non-synaptic interfaces.
evidence: This is a description of the test set used for SynEM evaluation.

claim: SynEM automatically classified the test set at 88% precision and recall.
source: SynEM automatically classified these at 88% precision and recall (Figure 3e, F1 score of 0.883).
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by experimental data and reference to Figure 3e.

claim: The majority of synapses in the cortex are made onto spines (87% in the test set).
source: Since the majority of synapses in the cortex are made onto spines we also evaluated SynEM on all spine synapses in the test set (n = 204 of 235 synapses, 87%, Figure 3e).
evidence: This is a factual statement about synapse distribution in the cortex, supported by data from the test set.

claim: On spine synapses, SynEM performed at 94% precision and 89% recall.
source: On these, SynEM performed even better, yielding 94% precision and 89% recall. (Figure 3e, F1 score of 0.914).
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by experimental data and reference to Figure 3e.

claim: SynEM outperforms the state-of-the-art methods when applied to SBEM data acquired at 3537 nm3 voxel size.
source: SynEM outperforms the state-of-the-art methods when applied to our SBEM data acquired at 3537 nm3 voxel size (Figure 3f, Figure 3—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by experimental data and reference to Figure 3f and Figure 3—figure supplement 3.

claim: SynEM outperforms the method developed for the ATUM dataset (VesicleCNN) when applied to that dataset.
source: In addition, we applied SynEM to a published 3D EM dataset acquired at more than 10-fold smaller voxel size (3 × 3 × 30 = 270 nm3) using automated tape-collecting ultramicrotome-SEM imaging (ATUM, Kasthuri et al., 2015). SynEM also outperforms the method developed for this data (VesicleCNN, Roncal et al., 2015; Figure 3f and Figure 3—figure supplement 4), indicating that SynEM is applicable to EM data of various modalities and resolution.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by experimental data and reference to Figure 3f and Figure 3—figure supplement 4, with citations to Kasthuri et al., 2015 and Roncal et al., 2015.

claim: SynEM is applicable to EM data of various modalities and resolution.
source: In addition, we applied SynEM to a published 3D EM dataset acquired at more than 10-fold smaller voxel size (3 × 3 × 30 = 270 nm3) using automated tape-collecting ultramicrotome-SEM imaging (ATUM, Kasthuri et al., 2015). SynEM also outperforms the method developed for this data (VesicleCNN, Roncal et al., 2015; Figure 3f and Figure 3—figure supplement 4), indicating that SynEM is applicable to EM data of various modalities and resolution.
evidence: This is an inference based on the performance of SynEM on different datasets.

claim: The recently published method (Dorkenwald et al., 2017) reported that the additional detection of the synaptic partners yielded a drop of performance of 2% precision and 9% recall compared to synapse detection alone.
source: Interestingly, the recently published method (Dorkenwald et al., 2017) reported that the additional detection of the synaptic partners yielded a drop of performance of 2% precision and 9% recall (F1 score decreased by about 5% from 0.906 to 0.849) compared to synapse detection alone (Figure 3f, see Dorkenwald et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Dorkenwald et al., 2017 and reference to Figure 3f.

claim: SynEM explicitly provides synapse detection, partner detection and synapse directionality in one classification step.
source: SynEM, because of the explicit classification of directed neurite interfaces, in contrast, explicitly provides synapse detection, partner detection and synapse directionality in one classification step.
evidence: This is a description of the SynEM approach and its advantages over other methods.

claim: 26 of the 28 false negatives and 22 of the 27 false positives in the test set were at locations with a SegEM error in proximity.
source: To estimate the effect of segmentation errors on SynEM performance, we investigated all false positive and false negative detections in the test set and checked for the local volume segmentation quality. We found that, in fact, 26 of the 28 FNs and 22 of the 27 FPs were at locations with a SegEM error in proximity.
evidence: This is a finding from the analysis of SynEM errors in the test set.

claim: Correcting segmentation errors corrected the SynEM errors in 22 of 48 (46%) of the cases.
source: Correcting these errors also corrected the SynEM errors in 22 of 48 (46%) of the cases.
evidence: This is a finding from the analysis of SynEM errors in the test set.

claim: Further improvement of volume segmentation can yield an even further reduction of the remaining errors in SynEM-based automated synapse detection.
source: This indicates that further improvement of volume segmentation can yield an even further reduction of the remaining errors in SynEM-based automated synapse detection.
evidence: This is an inference based on the analysis of SynEM errors and their relationship to segmentation errors.

claim: 378 out of 3224 features contributed to classification in SynEM.
source: 378 out of 3224 features contributed to classification (leaving out the remaining features did not reduce accuracy).
evidence: This is a finding from the analysis of feature importance in SynEM.

claim: The 10 features with highest discriminative power in SynEM contained two of the added texture filters (int-var and local entropy) and a shape feature.
source: The 10 features with highest discriminative power (Table 2) in fact contained two of the added texture filters (int-var and local entropy) and a shape feature.
evidence: This is a finding from the analysis of feature importance in SynEM, with reference to Table 2.

claim: The three most distinctive subvolumes in SynEM were the large presynaptic subvolume, the border and the small postsynaptic subvolume.
source: The three most distinctive subvolumes (Figure 4b) were the large presynaptic subvolume, the border and the small postsynaptic subvolume.
evidence: This is a finding from the analysis of feature importance in SynEM, with reference to Figure 4b.

claim: The asymmetry in pre- vs. postsynaptic aggregation volumes contributed to classification performance in SynEM.
source: This suggests that the asymmetry in pre- vs. postsynaptic aggregation volumes in fact contributed to classification performance, with a focus on the presynaptic vesicle cloud and the postsynaptic density.
evidence: This is an inference based on the analysis of feature importance in SynEM.

claim: SynEM is sufficiently computationally efficient to be applied to large connectomics datasets.
source: Finally, SynEM is sufficiently computationally efficient to be applied to large connectomics datasets.
evidence: This is a statement about the computational efficiency of SynEM, supported by runtime data.

claim: The total runtime of SynEM on the 384592 μm3 dataset was 2.6 hr on a mid-size computational cluster (480 CPU cores, 16 GB RAM per core).
source: The total runtime on the 384592 μm3 dataset was 2.6 hr on a mid-size computational cluster (480 CPU cores, 16 GB RAM per core).
evidence: This is a measurement of SynEM runtime on the dataset.

claim: The runtime for SynEM on a large 1 mm3 dataset would be 279.9 days.
source: This would imply a runtime of 279.9 days for a large 1 mm3 dataset, which is comparable to the time required for current segmentation methods, but much faster than the currently required human annotation time (105 to 106 hr, Figure 1c).
evidence: This is a calculation based on the measured runtime on the smaller dataset, with reference to Figure 1c.

claim: Synaptic connections between neurons in the mammalian cerebral cortex have been found to be established via multiple synapses per neuron pair.
source: Synaptic connections between neurons in the mammalian cerebral cortex have been found to be established via multiple synapses per neuron pair (Figure 5b, Feldmeyer et al., 1999, 2002, 2006; Frick et al., 2008; Markram et al., 1997, range 1–8 synapses per connection, mean 4.3 ± 1.4 for excitatory connections, Supplementary file 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to multiple studies (Feldmeyer et al., 1999, 2002, 2006; Frick et al., 2008; Markram et al., 1997) and reference to Figure 5b and Supplementary file 2.

claim: The range of synapses per excitatory connection is 1–8 synapses, with a mean of 4.3 ± 1.4.
source: Synaptic connections between neurons in the mammalian cerebral cortex have been found to be established via multiple synapses per neuron pair (Figure 5b, Feldmeyer et al., 1999, 2002, 2006; Frick et al., 2008; Markram et al., 1997, range 1–8 synapses per connection, mean 4.3 ± 1.4 for excitatory connections, Supplementary file 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to multiple studies (Feldmeyer et al., 1999, 2002, 2006; Frick et al., 2008; Markram et al., 1997) and reference to Supplementary file 2.

claim: For connectomes in which neuron pairs with at least one detected synapse are considered as connected (γnn = 1), a neuron-to-neuron connectivity recall Rnn of 97% can be achieved with a synapse detection recall Rs of 65.1%.
source: For connectomes in which neuron pairs with at least one detected synapse are considered as connected (γnn = 1), a neuron-to-neuron connectivity recall Rnn of 97% can be achieved with a synapse detection recall Rs of 65.1% (Figure 5c, black arrow) if synapse detection is independent between multiple synapses of the same neuron pair.
evidence: This is a calculation based on the statistical model of connectome errors, with reference to Figure 5c.

claim: SynEM achieves 99.4% synapse detection precision Ps at 65.1% recall.
source: SynEM achieves 99.4% synapse detection precision Ps at this recall (Figure 3e).
evidence: This is a finding from the SynEM evaluation, with reference to Figure 3e.

claim: At Rnn of 97.1%, SynEM yields a neuron-to-neuron connection precision Pnn of 98.5%.
source: At Rnn of 97.1%, SynEM yields a neuron-to-neuron connection precision Pnn of 98.5% (Figure 5d, black arrow, Figure 5e; note that this result is stable against varying underlying connectivity rates cre = 5%..30%, see indicated ranges in Figure 5e).
evidence: This is a calculation based on the statistical model of connectome errors, with reference to Figure 5d and Figure 5e.

claim: The precision and recall for single inhibitory synapses is 75% recall and 82% precision.
source: For this, we evaluated SynEM on a test set of inhibitory axons for which we classified all neurite contacts of these axons (171 synapses, 9430 interfaces). While the precision and recall for single inhibitory synapses is lower than for excitatory ones (75% recall, 82% precision, Figure 5—figure supplement 1, SynEM(i)s), the higher number of synapses per connected cell pair (n(i)syn is on average about 6, Supplementary file 3, Gupta et al. (2000); Markram et al. (2004); Koelbl et al. (2015); Hoffmann et al. (2015)) still yields substantial neuron-to-neuron precision and recall also for inhibitory connectomes (98% recall, 97% precision, Figure 5e, Figure 5—figure supplement 1, SynEM(i)nn; this result is stable against varying underlying inhibitory connectivity rates cri = 20%..80%, see ranges indicated in Figure 5e).
evidence: This is a finding from the SynEM evaluation on inhibitory synapses, with reference to Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

evidence: This claim is supported by citations to multiple studies (Gupta et al., 2000; Markram et al., 2004; Koelbl et al., 2015; Hoffmann et al., 2015) and reference to Supplementary file 3.

source: For this, we evaluated SynEM on a test set of inhibitory axons for which we classified all neurite contacts of these axons (171 synapses, 9430 interfaces). evidence: This is a calculation based on the statistical model of connectome errors, with reference to Figure 5e and Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: Error rates of less than 3% for missed connections and for wrongly detected connections are well below the noise of synaptic connectivity so far found in real biological circuits.
source: Error rates of less than 3% for missed connections and for wrongly detected connections are well below the noise of synaptic connectivity so far found in real biological circuits (e.g., Helmstaedter et al., 2013; Bartol et al., 2015), and thus likely sufficient for a large range of studies involving the mapping of cortical connectomes.
evidence: This is a statement about the biological significance of the error rates, supported by citations to Helmstaedter et al., 2013 and Bartol et al., 2015.

claim: SynEM provides fully automated detection of synapses, their synaptic partner neurites and synapse direction for binary mammalian connectomes up to 97% precision and recall.
source: In summary, SynEM provides fully automated detection of synapses, their synaptic partner neurites and synapse direction for binary mammalian connectomes up to 97% precision and recall, a range which was previously prohibitively expensive to attain in large-scale volumes by existing methods (Figure 5e, Figure 5—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is a summary of the primary findings of the study, with reference to Figure 5e and Figure 5—figure supplement 2.

claim: SynEM was applied to a sparse local cortical connectome between 104 axons and 100 postsynaptic processes in the dataset from L4 of mouse cortex.
source: We applied SynEM to a sparse local cortical connectome between 104 axons and 100 postsynaptic processes in the dataset from L4 of mouse cortex (Figure 6a, neurites were reconstructed using webKnossos (Boergens et al., 2017) and SegEM as previously reported (Berning et al., 2015)).
evidence: This is a description of the application of SynEM to a local connectome, with reference to Figure 6a and citations to webKnossos and SegEM.

claim: The resulting connectome contained 880 synapses distributed over 536 connections.
source: The resulting connectome contained 880 synapses distributed over 536 connections.
evidence: This is a finding from the application of SynEM to the local connectome.

claim: SynEM detected 195644 synapses in half of the entire cortex dataset (192296 µm3), yielding a synapse density of 1.02 synapses per µm3.
source: Finally, to check whether SynEM-detected synapses matched previous reports on synapse frequency and size, we applied SynEM to half of the entire cortex dataset used for this study (i.e. a volume of 192296 µm3). SynEM detected 195644 synapses, i.e. a synapse density of 1.02 synapses per µm3, consistent with previous reports (Merchán-Pérez et al., 2014).
evidence: This is a finding from the application of SynEM to a large volume, with citation to Merchán-Pérez et al., 2014.

claim: The synapse density of 1.02 synapses per µm3 detected by SynEM is consistent with previous reports.
source: Finally, to check whether SynEM-detected synapses matched previous reports on synapse frequency and size, we applied SynEM to half of the entire cortex dataset used for this study (i.e. a volume of 192296 µm3). SynEM detected 195644 synapses, i.e. a synapse density of 1.02 synapses per µm3, consistent with previous reports (Merchán-Pérez et al., 2014).
evidence: This is a comparison of SynEM results to previous reports, with citation to Merchán-Pérez et al., 2014.

claim: The average axon-spine interface size of SynEM detected synapses is 0.263 ± 0.206 µm2 (mean ± s.d.; range 0.033–1.189 µm2; n = 181).
source: We then measured the size of the axon-spine interface of SynEM detected synapses in the test set (Figure 7a,b). We find an average axon-spine interface size of 0.263 ± 0.206 µm2 (mean ± s.d.; range 0.033–1.189 µm2; n = 181), consistent with previous reports (de Vivo et al., 2017: (SW) 0.297 ± 0.297 µm2 (p=0.518, two-sample two-tailed t-test on the natural logarithm of the axon-spine interface size), (EW) 0.284 ± 0.275 µm2 (p=0.826, two-sample two-tailed t-test on the natural logarithm of the axon-spine interface size).
evidence: This is a measurement of synapse size from SynEM-detected synapses, with reference to Figure 7a,b and citation to de Vivo et al., 2017.

claim: The axon-spine interface size distribution of SynEM-detected synapses is consistent with previous reports from higher-resolution data.
source: We then measured the size of the axon-spine interface of SynEM detected synapses in the test set (Figure 7a,b). We find an average axon-spine interface size of 0.263 ± 0.206 µm2 (mean ± s.d.; range 0.033–1.189 µm2; n = 181), consistent with previous reports (de Vivo et al., 2017: (SW) 0.297 ± 0.297 µm2 (p=0.518, two-sample two-tailed t-test on the natural logarithm of the axon-spine interface size), (EW) 0.284 ± 0.275 µm2 (p=0.826, two-sample two-tailed t-test on the natural logarithm of the axon-spine interface size). This indicates that, first, synapse detection in our lower-resolution SBEM data (in-plane image resolution about 11 nm, section thickness about 26–30 nm) yields similar synapse size distributions as in the higher-resolution data in de Vivo et al. (2017) (in-plane image resolution 5.9 nm; section thickness about 50 nm) and secondly, that SynEM-based synapse detection has no obvious bias towards larger synapses.
evidence: This is a comparison of SynEM results to previous reports, with citation to de Vivo et al., 2017.

claim: SynEM-based synapse detection has no obvious bias towards larger synapses.

evidence: This is an inference based on the comparison of synapse size distributions.

claim: The particular achievement of SynEM is that the synapse detection for densely mapped connectomes from the mammalian cerebral cortex is fully automated yielding below 3% residual error in the binary connectome.
source: We report SynEM, a toolset for automated synapse detection in EM-based connectomics. The particular achievement is that the synapse detection for densely mapped connectomes from the mammalian cerebral cortex is fully automated yielding below 3% residual error in the binary connectome.
evidence: This is a summary of the primary achievement of the study.

claim: SynEM directly provides the location and size of synapses, the involved neurites and the synapse direction without human interaction.
source: Importantly, SynEM directly provides the location and size of synapses, the involved neurites and the synapse direction without human interaction.
evidence: This is a description of the capabilities of SynEM.

claim: With SynEM, synapse detection is removed as a bottleneck in large-scale mammalian connectomics.
source: With this, synapse detection is removed as a bottleneck in large-scale mammalian connectomics.
evidence: This is a conclusion about the impact of SynEM on the field of connectomics.

claim: Synapse detection is facilitated in high-resolution EM data, and becomes most feasible in FIB-SEM data at a resolution of about 4–8 nm isotropic.
source: Evidently, synapse detection is facilitated in high-resolution EM data, and becomes most feasible in FIB-SEM data at a resolution of about 4–8 nm isotropic (Kreshuk et al., 2011, Figure 3f).
evidence: This is a statement about the relationship between imaging resolution and synapse detection, with citation to Kreshuk et al., 2011 and reference to Figure 3f.

claim: Only by compromising resolution for speed (and thus volume) of imaging, the mapping of large, potentially even whole-brain connectomes is becoming plausible.
source: Yet, only by compromising resolution for speed (and thus volume) of imaging, the mapping of large, potentially even whole-brain connectomes is becoming plausible (Figure 3f).
evidence: This is a statement about the trade-offs in EM imaging for connectomics, with reference to Figure 3f.

claim: The fact that SynEM also outperforms state-of-the-art methods on high-resolution anisotropic 3D EM data indicates that the approach of segmentation-based interface classification has merits in a wider range of 3D EM data modalities.
source: The fact that SynEM also outperforms state-of-the-art methods on high-resolution anisotropic 3D EM data (Figure 3f, Roncal et al., 2015) indicates that our approach of segmentation-based interface classification has merits in a wider range of 3D EM data modalities.
evidence: This is an inference based on the performance of SynEM on different datasets, with reference to Figure 3f and citation to Roncal et al., 2015.

claim: Special fixation procedures that enhance the extracellular space in 3D EM data are reported to simplify synapse detection for human annotators.
source: In addition to high image resolution, recently proposed special fixation procedures that enhance the extracellular space in 3D EM data (Pallotto et al., 2015) are reported to simplify synapse detection for human annotators.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Pallotto et al., 2015.

claim: In data with enhanced extracellular space, direct touch between neurites has a very high predictive power for the existence of a (chemical or electrical) synapse.
source: In such data, direct touch between neurites has a very high predictive power for the existence of a (chemical or electrical) synapse, since otherwise neurite boundaries are separated by extracellular space.
evidence: This is a statement about the properties of data with enhanced extracellular space, based on logical inference.

claim: It is expected that data with enhanced extracellular space also substantially simplifies automated synapse detection.
source: Thus, it is expected that such data also substantially simplifies automated synapse detection.
evidence: This is a speculation about the potential benefits of enhanced extracellular space for automated synapse detection.

claim: The advantage of SynEM is that it achieves fully automated synapse detection in conventionally stained and fixated 3D EM data.
source: The advantage of SynEM is that it achieves fully automated synapse detection in conventionally stained and fixated 3D EM data, in which neurite contact is most frequent at non-synaptic sites.
evidence: This is a statement about the advantages of SynEM compared to methods that require special fixation.

claim: Conventionally stained and fixated 3D EM data are widely used.
source: Such data are widely used, and acquiring such data does not require special fixation protocols.
evidence: This is a statement about the prevalence of conventionally stained and fixated 3D EM data, based on established knowledge.

claim: With the increasing availability of large-scale 3D EM datasets, synapse types can be defined based on multiple synapses of the same axon.
source: So far, the classification of synapses into inhibitory (symmetric) vs. excitatory (asymmetric) was carried out for a given single synapse, often in single cross sections of single synapses (e.g. Colonnier, 1968). With the increasing availability of large-scale 3D EM datasets, however, synapse types can be defined based on multiple synapses of the same axon (e.g. Kasthuri et al., 2015).
evidence: This is a statement about the changing approach to synapse classification with large-scale datasets, with citations to Colonnier, 1968 and Kasthuri et al., 2015.

claim: In a dataset sized a cubic millimeter of cortical tissue, most axons of interneurons will be fully contained in the dataset since most inhibitory neurons are local.
source: In the case of a dataset sized a cubic millimeter of cortical tissue, most axons of interneurons will be fully contained in the dataset since most inhibitory neurons are local.
evidence: This is a statement about the properties of large-scale datasets, based on established knowledge of cortical anatomy.

claim: The classification of single synapses can be replaced by the assignment of synapses to the respective axon; the type of axon is then inferred from the neurons' somatic and dendritic features.
source: Consequently, the classification of single synapses can be replaced by the assignment of synapses to the respective axon; the type of axon is then inferred from the neurons' somatic and dendritic features.
evidence: This is a description of an alternative approach to synapse classification in large-scale datasets.

claim: Even for axons which are not completely contained in the dataset, the assignment to inhibitory or excitatory synaptic phenotypes can be based on dozens or hundreds rather than single synapses.
source: Even for axons which are not completely contained in the dataset, the assignment to inhibitory or excitatory synaptic phenotypes can be based on dozens or hundreds rather than single synapses.
evidence: This is a statement about the advantages of large-scale datasets for synapse classification.

claim: SynEM resolves synapse detection for high-throughput cortical connectomics of mammalian brains, removing synapse detection as a bottleneck in connectomics.
source: Together, SynEM resolves synapse detection for high-throughput cortical connectomics of mammalian brains, removing synapse detection as a bottleneck in connectomics.
evidence: This is a summary of the impact of SynEM on the field of connectomics.

claim: With SynEM, the further acceleration of neurite reconstruction is again the key challenge for future connectomic analysis.
source: With this, SynEM renders the further acceleration of neurite reconstruction again the key challenge for future connectomic analysis.
evidence: This is a statement about the implications of SynEM for future work in connectomics.
